title: When Work Follows You Home: Switching Off in an Always-On Job
excerpt: Why it's so hard to switch off, what always-on work does to your nervous system, and practical ways to reclaim your evenings.

value.text: You close the laptop, but work does not close with you. The evening arrives and your mind is still drafting the reply you did not send, rehearsing tomorrow's meeting, half-listening for the ping that might need you. You are physically home, yet some part of you never quite left the office. If switching off has started to feel like a skill you have lost, you are far from alone.

Always-on work is not simply a matter of long hours. It is the low, constant expectation that you could be reached — that a message might arrive, that something might need you, that you should probably just check. And it is precisely that open loop, more than the work itself, that quietly wears people down.
Why switching off is genuinely hard

Switching off is difficult because your job has trained you not to. When responsiveness is rewarded and delay carries a cost, staying alert stops being a choice and becomes a habit your body has learned. The phone in your pocket is a doorway your workplace can walk through at any hour, and part of you stays braced for it.

For conscientious, capable people this is especially sticky. The very qualities that make you good at your work — care, reliability, not wanting to let people down — are the ones that make it hardest to put the work down. Rest can start to feel like risk, as though relaxing your grip is the moment something will go wrong.
What always-on does to your nervous system

Your nervous system is built to mobilise for a demand and then return to rest once it passes. Always-on work removes the second half of that rhythm. The demand never fully ends, so the system never gets the clear signal that it is safe to stand down. Instead of alternating between effort and recovery, you hover in a state of low-grade readiness that rarely switches off.
Over time that constant readiness shows up in the body and mood — often in ways that are easy to blame on personality or a busy stretch rather than on how work is structured.

items: Sleep that comes late or breaks up, with the mind restarting the moment your head hits the pillow.
A wired-but-tired feeling — exhausted, yet unable to properly settle.
Difficulty being fully present with the people you are actually with.
A shortening fuse: small frustrations landing harder than they should.
Downtime that does not restore, because part of you stays on standby.

value.text: These are not signs that you are coping badly. They are what a nervous system looks like when it has not been allowed to complete the return to rest for a long time.

You may not be able to change your industry's culture overnight, but you can create real edges around the demand — and the point of an edge is less about strict rules than about giving your nervous system a reliable signal that the day's readiness can now end.

items: Build a shutdown ritual: a short, repeatable act — a walk, a closing note for tomorrow, changing clothes — that tells your body the workday is over.
Make one clear boundary and keep it, rather than many you cannot sustain. A consistent "no messages after 8" teaches your system more than a fragile all-day plan.
Move notifications off the devices you rest with, so checking becomes a decision rather than a reflex.
Protect a genuinely off-limits window and defend it as you would a meeting.
Give the day an ending it can hear. Nervous systems settle to signals, not intentions.

value.text: If this pattern has become the water you swim in, working through it with support can help you find boundaries that actually fit your life — you can see how I work with individuals on the [work together](/work-with-me) page. Change here is rarely about doing more; it is about letting the day properly end.
When it's the culture, not just you

It is worth naming plainly that always-on strain is often built into how a team or organisation operates, not into any individual's willpower. If everyone is expected to be reachable, no one can switch off — and no amount of personal discipline fully solves a shared problem. That is why I also work with teams and employers on wellbeing and sustainable ways of working, which you can read about on the [organisations](/organisations) page.

Your evenings are not a luxury you have to earn by finishing everything first — the work is rarely ever finished. They are the part of the day where you get to be a person rather than a role. Learning to let work end at the door is not about caring less. It is about staying well enough to keep caring at all.
